title: The Ocean That Isn’t There
find: A slick olive-green cobble two rows in from the kerb, darker than everything around it when wet.
look: Waxy olive-green, soapy to the touch, cut by pale veins that meet at odd angles. The green is water — chemically bound into the mineral when seawater met hot ocean crust.
story: Before New England existed there was an ocean called Iapetus. This stone is a piece of its floor, hydrated at a spreading ridge and later scraped onto a continent instead of being swallowed.

chapters.label: An ocean with no coastline left

title: The First Collision
find: Look for the cobble that flashes silver when you move your head — it only shines in one direction.
look: Silvery sheets of mica lying all one way, and blood-red garnets the size of peppercorns sitting proud of the surface where the softer minerals wore away.
story: An island arc ran aground on ancient North America. Mud on the sea floor was buried, cooked and squeezed until its minerals grew in rows — the rock remembers the direction of the squeeze.

chapters.label: Why the mica all lies one way

title: A Continent Called Avalonia
find: Third row from the gutter on the harbour side — the coolest, bluest grey stone in the row.
look: Cool blue-grey and evenly speckled. The dark needles are riebeckite, an amphibole that only grows in dry alkali magma — rare, and a fingerprint of where this came from.
story: Half of eastern New England is a foreign continent. Avalonia drifted in from the southern hemisphere and docked; its granites are the basement under Boston, quarried later for pavement.

chapters.label: A continent arrives from the south

title: Everything Welds Shut
find: The banded stone with pale swirls, near the elm on the north side.
look: Bands folded like taffy. The pale streaks were molten while the dark ones stayed solid — a rock caught halfway to becoming magma.
story: Africa closed in and Pangaea welded together. Deep under the collision, rock got hot enough to partly melt, and the melt wandered a few centimetres before freezing where you see it.

title: The Crack That Became an Ocean
find: Almost black, and noticeably heavier underfoot — it rings differently when a cart crosses it.
look: Near-black, dense, faintly pitted. A hand lens finds glassy laths of feldspar crossing a dark ground — magma that cooled fast in a crack.
story: Pangaea tore back apart along the seam it had welded. Magma filled the cracks. The Atlantic began as a rift valley, and this stone was in its wall.

title: Carried Here by Ice
find: A rounded stone with fine parallel scratches on its upper face — catch it in low sun.
look: Rounded on every face, speckled black and white, and scored with a set of fine parallel scratches. That is the ice’s own handwriting, made by grit dragged under a glacier.
story: Nantucket is a pile of debris left where the ice stopped. This stone was quarried by a glacier somewhere north of here and set down when the ice melted out from under it.

title: Laid by Hand, 1837
find: Squarer than its neighbours, with tool marks on two faces.
look: Squarer than everything around it, with tool marks on two faces. This one was quarried, not found — it crossed water in a ship’s belly as ballast.
story: The last chapter is ours. Nantucket paved Main Street with stone brought in by sea, and in doing so built a floor of deep time that the whole town walks over without looking down.
